newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul to seek tough U.S. stand against N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: Seoul to seek tough U.S. stand against N.Korea.

text.p: South Korea will seek a tough U.S stand against the Stalinist North despite Pyongyang's apparent shelving of a planned missile test, government officials said on Friday.

They said a decision to halt the test will not remove the threat to regional stability, and that the South Korean president Kim Young-sam would discuss the issue with U.S. President Bill Clinton when the two meet later this month.
A senior U.S State Departement official said on Thursday that Washington had strongly opposed North Korea's planned ballistic missile test as a threat to regional stability.

"We believe that they were making those preparations (for a medium range missile test) and that they've now stopped the preparations," said Charles Kartman, deputy assistant secretary of state for East Asian affairs.

"President Kim Young-sam and President (Bill) Clinton are due to meet during an APEC meeting this month, and the submarine incident and the question of the stability on the Korean peninsula will feature high," an aide to Kim told Reuters.
Tension has remained high on the peninsula, the world's last Cold War frontier, since a submarine landed 26 North Koreans in September off the eastern city of Kangnung.

"North Korean provocations are a serious security threat to the peninsula and the region, and President Kim will seek to reaffirm strong alliance with the U.S. against the threat," said the aide, who is involved in formulating Seoul's foreign policy.
"We have demanded a clear apology (by the North) over the submarine intrusion and steps to prevent the repetition of such an incident. We maintain the position," he said.
Clinton and Kim are due to hold a separate meeting during the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in the Philippines later this month.

Last month, the State Department said it had sent a "very strong message" to North Korea not to carry out the test for fear of stoking instability in the region by advancing its extensive ballistic missile development programme.

Washington has said it is concerned over any testing that might promote North Korean missile sales to the Middle East and other unstable areas. Pyongyang last test-fired a medium-range ballistic missile into waters off Japan in 1993.
"We are not sure if North Korea is suspending the preparation of the test or calling it off for good," a senior official at South Korea's Foreign Ministry said.
"Shelving the missile test will not remove threats to the stability of the region. North Korea should end provocative activities and seek genuine detente," he said.
The official said the submarine intrusion was a clear indication that North Korea was still trying to take the South by force.
The submarine ran aground off Kangnung on September 17 as it tried to pick up three spies it had offloaded two days earlier, the only North Korean captured alive from the vessel said later.
Seoul officials have said that of the 26 North Korean infiltrators, 13 were shot dead, one captured and eleven others killed themselves. One is still at large.
South Korea has said it does not want to isolate North Korea but stressed it could not cooperate with the Stalinst state as long as it pursued hostile policies towards the South.

Yu Suk-ryul, a senior fellow at the Seoul government-backed Institute of Foreign Affairs and National Security, said he believed North Korea's apparent decision to halt the missile test was an overture of cooperation to the United States.

"North Korea's economy is in a bad shape. It wants the United States to ease economic sanctions and help secure Western capital, but Seoul tries to link the improvement of U.S.-North Korean ties with that of North-South (Korean) ties," Yu said.
